title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
subtitle: Encoding binary data as printable ASCII text

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4648 defines the Base16, Base32 and Base64 encodings, which turn arbitrary binary data into text made of a restricted set of printable characters. This lets binary data travel through text-only channels such as email, URLs and JSON. Base64 is the most common of the three.

questions: why does base64 end with equals signs
what is the difference between base64 and base64url

tldr.problem: Many channels, such as email and URLs, can only carry a limited set of printable characters, but data is arbitrary bytes.
tldr.mechanism: Split the bytes into 6-, 5- or 4-bit groups and map each group to a character in a 64-, 32- or 16-character alphabet, padding with = when needed.
tldr.outcome: Any binary data can travel as text, at a cost in size, and Base64 became the default way to do it.

today: Base64 is everywhere: MIME email attachments, data: URIs, HTTP Basic authentication, PEM-encoded certificates and keys, and JSON Web Tokens, which use the base64url form without padding. Base16 is the usual way to print hashes and byte dumps, and Base32 appears where case-insensitivity matters. Encoding is not encryption, because anyone can decode it.

hero.subtitle: Encoding binary data as printable ASCII text

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Base encodings convert arbitrary binary data into text using a restricted alphabet of printable ASCII characters. This is essential for transporting binary data through text-only channels such as email, URLs, and JSON.

Base64 is by far the most commonly used encoding. You encounter it in email attachments (MIME), data URIs, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), HTTP Basic authentication, and embedded images in CSS/HTML.
sections.plainLanguage: Base encodings convert binary data into text using a restricted alphabet of printable ASCII characters. This allows binary data to pass through text-only channels such as email, URLs and JSON. Base64 is the most common. It appears in email attachments, data URIs, JSON Web Tokens and HTTP Basic authentication.

sections.title: Base64 Encoding
sections.content:
Base64 encoding groups input bytes into 24-bit blocks (3 bytes), then splits each block into four 6-bit groups. Each 6-bit value indexes into the Base64 alphabet to produce a printable character.

Base64 Alphabet
Value  Char   Value  Char   Value  Char   Value  Char
  0    A       16    Q       32    g       48    w
  1    B       17    R       33    h       49    x
  2    C       18    S       34    i       50    y
  3    D       19    T       35    j       51    z
  4    E       20    U       36    k       52    0
  5    F       21    V       37    l       53    1
  ...  ...     ...   ...     ...   ...     ...   ...
 25    Z       41    p       57    5       63    /

Padding character: =
Encoding Example: "Man"
Text:    M           a           n
ASCII:   77          97          110
Binary:  01001101    01100001    01101110

6-bit:   010011  010110  000101  101110
Value:   19      22      5       46
Base64:  T       W       F       u

Result: "Man" -> "TWFu"
sections.plainLanguage: Base64 splits input into 3-byte (24-bit) blocks and divides each block into four 6-bit groups. Each group selects one printable character from a 64-character alphabet. For example, the text "Man" becomes "TWFu".

sections.title: Base32 Encoding
sections.content:
Base32 uses a 32-character alphabet (A-Z and 2-7) and groups data into 5-bit chunks. It is less space-efficient than Base64 but uses only uppercase letters and digits, making it suitable for case-insensitive contexts.

sections.plainLanguage: Base32 uses a 32-character alphabet (A to Z and 2 to 7) and 5-bit groups. It takes more space than Base64, with 60 percent expansion against 33 percent, but it uses only uppercase letters and digits. That makes it suitable where case is not preserved.

sections.title: Base16 (Hex) Encoding
sections.content:
Base16 uses the hexadecimal digits 0-9 and A-F. Each byte is represented by exactly two hex characters. While it doubles the data size, it provides direct byte-level inspection.

Base16 Examples
"Hello" -> 48656C6C6F
"Man"   -> 4D616E
\x00    -> 00
\xff    -> FF

Base16 is commonly used for displaying cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, MD5), MAC addresses (00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E), and debugging binary protocols. It is case-insensitive per this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Base16 is hexadecimal: each byte becomes exactly two characters from 0 to 9 and A to F. It doubles the data size but lets you read each byte directly. It is commonly used to display hashes and MAC addresses and to debug binary protocols. It is case-insensitive in this specification.

sections.title: Padding
sections.content:
When the input length is not evenly divisible by the group size, padding characters (=) are appended to the output.

Base64, 0 remainingNo padding needed
Base64, 1 remainingTwo = characters appended
Base64, 2 remainingOne = character appended
Padding Examples
"Man"    -> "TWFu"     (3 bytes = no padding)
"Ma"     -> "TWE="     (2 bytes = 1 pad)
"M"      -> "TQ=="     (1 byte  = 2 pads)
sections.plainLanguage: When the input length does not divide evenly into the encoding's groups, the output is padded with = characters. In Base64, one leftover byte gives two = and two leftover bytes give one. For example, "Ma" becomes "TWE=" and "M" becomes "TQ==".

sections.title: URL-Safe Base64 Variant
sections.content:
The standard Base64 alphabet includes + and / which have special meaning in URLs. The URL-safe variant (base64url) replaces these characters.

+ replaced by -Plus sign is replaced with hyphen/minusIndex 62
/ replaced by _Forward slash is replaced with underscoreIndex 63

The base64url encoding is required by several modern standards including JSON Web Tokens (JWT/JWS/JWE) and OAuth 2.0 PKCE. Padding may be omitted in contexts where the data length is known.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard Base64 uses + and /, which have special meaning in URLs. The URL-safe variant, base64url, replaces them with - and _. Padding may be omitted when the data length is known. JSON Web Tokens and OAuth 2.0 PKCE require this variant.
